tools: Fits a straight line (or plane) by least squares: learns coef_ and intercept_.
The first model for a numeric target; here, minutes from distance.
Predicts from the k nearest training rows (vote or average). k = 1 memorizes the training data.
Quick flexible baseline; demonstrates memorizing vs generalizing.
Do-nothing models: most frequent class, class priors, mean, median… strategy="prior" is the classifier default.
Always, first: the score every real model must beat.
Saves and loads fitted Python objects such as a whole Pipeline (joblib.dump, joblib.load). Only load files you trust.
Shipping a trained model to a batch job or service.
Splits unlabelled rows into k groups around k centres.
Spread the few known labels to unlabelled rows (marked −1) along a similarity graph.
Few labels, many unlabelled rows, classes that follow the data's shape.
Wraps a classifier that labels its own most confident predictions and retrains.
Semi-supervised learning with any probabilistic classifier.
Fits and scores a fresh copy of the estimator on k train/test splits and returns the k scores.
Comparing candidates (rule, linear, trees) on equal terms; honest scores for small data.
Fast gradient-boosted trees with binned features, native missing values and categorical support.
The strong default for tabular data.
Learns yes/no questions on features; max_depth=1 learns a one-question rule.
Readable models; checking how far one rule gets you.
Learns each column's mean_ and scale_ in fit, then maps x to (x − mean) ÷ scale.
Before distance- or gradient-based models (k-NN, logistic regression).
Linear classifier with probabilities via predict_proba. In 1.9 penalty is deprecated in favour of l1_ratio.
Chains transformers and a final estimator into one estimator; fit runs fit_transform on each step in order, predict runs transform then predict.
Always: keeps preprocessing fitted on training data only and ships as one object.
Copies an estimator's hyperparameters without any learned state.
Getting a fresh, unfitted model (what cross-validation does internally).
transformer.set_output(transform="pandas") (since 1.2) makes transform return DataFrames with column names; also "polars".
Shuffles and splits arrays into train and test parts (default test_size 0.25); stratify=y keeps class shares.
Making train / validation / test piles (call it twice).
Keeps the k columns with the best univariate scores (e.g. f_classif). Must be fitted inside the training data.
Reducing many columns; a classic leak if fitted on all rows.
Cross-validation folds that keep all rows of a group (patient, user) on the same side.
Folds that always train on earlier rows and test on later ones.
acronyms: Learning a function from examples instead of writing the rules by hand.
Average size of the prediction errors, ignoring their sign, in the target's units.
Predict from the k closest training examples; k = 1 is a pure memorizer.
Learning which actions to take from rewards received after acting, often delayed.
Google's 2018 language model, pre-trained by predicting 15% masked word pieces.
A very large neural network pre-trained (self-supervised) to predict text, then fine-tuned.
LLM APIs, the sibling AI Engineer course
The tool sales and support teams use to track customers; a common place to deliver churn scores.
The engineering of running models: pipelines, tracking, registries, serving, monitoring, retraining.
Word counts weighted down for words that appear in many documents.
Splits one prediction into each feature's contribution.
Unsupervised method that squeezes many columns into a few directions that keep the most variation.
Repeated train/test splits of the training data to score or choose models without touching the test set.
terms: One past case to learn from: its features and, in supervised learning, its label.
A measurable input known at prediction time (a column of X).
The right answer for an example (y).
A family of functions plus the parameters learned for it.
A number the algorithm learns from data (a weight, a split threshold); attributes ending in _ in scikit-learn.
A setting you choose before training (k, max_depth, C), passed to the constructor.
Running the algorithm that chooses the parameters from examples.
The model's output for an input.
Doing well on inputs the model never saw; what held-out scores measure.
Fitting the training data's noise: great training score, worse on new data (e.g. k = 1).
A model too rigid to capture the real pattern (e.g. a straight line on curved data, huge k).
Learning from examples that all have labels.
Finding structure (groups, directions, oddities) in data without labels.
Learning from a few labelled and many unlabelled examples.
Supervised learning on labels made from the data itself (next word, masked word, hidden image patch).
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a small labelled dataset for your task.
Grouping unlabelled rows by similarity; clusters need not match the classes you care about.
The score of the simplest reasonable predictor (majority class, mean, a rule); every model must beat it.
The loop: frame → data and labels → features → model → evaluate → deploy → monitor → retrain.
When live features are computed differently from training features, so the deployed model sees different inputs.
The data (or its relation to the label) changes after deployment, so a fixed model decays.
Scores computed on a schedule into a table vs computed per request by a service.
Hand-written logic; best when exact, stable and known, or before you have data.
Any scikit-learn object that learns from data with fit.
An estimator with predict (and usually score).
An estimator with transform: turns data into new data using what fit learned.
fit then transform on the same data in one call; only for training data.
Class probabilities, one column per class in classes_ order.
The error raised when predict or transform is called before fit.
The rows used to fit the model and any preprocessing.
Held-out rows used to choose hyperparameters, features or models.
Held-out rows used once, at the end, for an honest estimate.
Information unavailable at prediction time (test rows, the future, the label) influencing training or model choice, inflating scores.
A feature created by, or after, the outcome (refund issued, retention offer sent).
Using future data to predict the past, e.g. a random split of time-ordered rows.
Copies or related rows (same patient, same user, augmented images) on both sides of a split.
Choosing models or settings by test score, which makes that score optimistic.
A split that keeps the class proportions the same in each part.
